editorNote: The final week of 1983 puts IBM’s long-awaited home computer under a reviewer’s lamp while Apple and Microsoft press graphical machines toward the office.
morningLine: Junior arrives for inspection as the home-computer price war closes out a turbulent year.

lead.headline: The Little IBM Finally Arrives for Its Test
lead.dek: PCjr leaves the brochure and meets the reviewer, with color, sound, PC DOS—and a long list of extras.
body: IBM’s bid for the family room finally moved from announcement-stage promise to hands-on judgment this week. In a December 27 test, the New York Times examined the PCjr as a real machine rather than a specification sheet, asking whether the most famous name in business computing could translate its success to the home.

Junior keeps close to the IBM PC family with an Intel 8088-class processor and PC DOS, but adds enhanced color and sound for games, education, and household software. IBM’s brochure calls it “The easy one for everyone,” an appeal that places entertainment and schoolwork alongside writing, spreadsheets, and communications.

The entry model combines 64K with cassette storage for $669. A 128K machine with a disk drive lists at $1,269, before a monitor and many practical accessories. That makes the sticker price only the opening calculation for a household comparing Junior with sharply discounted Commodore and Atari machines.

The infrared Freeboard keyboard removes the cord but gives the machine one of its most conspicuous departures from the office PC. Its compact keys and the system’s constrained expansion scheme are likely to matter as much as the bright graphics when buyers decide whether IBM compatibility is worth the compromise.

PCjr therefore reaches stores carrying two burdens: it must feel friendly enough for first-time owners and compatible enough to borrow the IBM PC’s authority. The holiday test is over for 1983, but the market test has only begun.

stories.headline: Lisa Opens a Line to IBM and DEC
body: Apple is giving the Lisa a way into computer rooms already dominated by larger systems. LisaTerminal can emulate DEC VT100 and VT52 terminals as well as IBM 3278 terminals, UPI reported Wednesday.

Together with Apple’s Cluster Controller, the software lets Lisa users reach information and applications on IBM hosts and DEC minicomputers. The move answers a practical corporate objection to the costly graphical workstation: a new desktop cannot remain an island.

stories.headline: Christmas Computer Boom Leaves a Price-War Hangover
body: The year ends with home computers more visible—and less expensive—than ever. COMPUTE! found Commodore 64 street prices below $200 and VIC-20 machines below $100 as manufacturers fought for mass-market volume.

The bargains came with bruises. Commodore shortages affected computers and disk drives, Coleco’s delayed Adam lost precious holiday time, and retailers faced returns as newcomers discovered that a complete working system often required more than the box under the tree.

Future Computing estimated monthly shipments of 160,000 machines for Commodore, 100,000 for Texas Instruments, 65,000 for Atari, and 35,000 for Radio Shack. The shake-out has enlarged the audience while making survival harder for the companies supplying it.

stories.headline: Windows Proposes One Face for DOS Programs
stories.confidence: Same-month BYTE coverage of a pre-release system.
body: Microsoft’s proposed Windows environment offers tiled program windows, common menus, device handling, and mouse control above the growing base of MS-DOS machines. BYTE’s December coverage gives readers an early look at software meant to make unlike programs behave more consistently.

The system is still a promise rather than a store-shelf product, with Microsoft projecting availability in 1984. It joins Visi On and other graphical environments in a contest to decide whether the next PC interface will be learned by typing commands or pointing at choices.

stories.headline: Atari Finds a Holiday Bright Spot
body: Electronic Games Hotline’s final pre-Christmas issue reported a welcome boom in Atari hardware and software sales. The note offers a useful view from the shop floor during a year more often defined by excess inventory and corporate retrenchment.

One strong holiday report cannot settle the industry’s problems, but cartridges and computer games still command attention. Ultima III, Lode Runner, and M.U.L.E. show how ambitious disk software is broadening play beyond the familiar console formula.
